So this was an interesting thread on LinkedIn over the past few days I thought worth summarizing, just some learnings.
And so there’s two pieces of advice, really, two big things you can do to increase your odds of making better hires when you’re hiring VPs, directors, whatever it is. And it turns out they go together. But they go against conventional wisdom today. So the first piece of advice is hire folks who are still hands-on, still do the work themselves. This seems obvious for junior hires, but less so for more senior ones. But we know it’s true, right? We all know it’s true. You want someone running sales ops to also be able to code up a dash board. Someone managing engineering to also ship product. Or something like that. That’s obviously important for junior roles. But what about senior leadership?
I think most founders would agree, sort of. They’d say yes, they want their senior leaders to still be able to roll up their sleeves, even if sometimes they don’t need to anymore. But here’s my learning:
if you hire someone to lead sales whose last experience wasn’t building a team, leading from the front—then they probably won’t succeed. Same thing for marketing. For support. Whatever it is. Now I’m not saying you shouldn’t hire people that aren’t technical. Because if you haven’t done it yourself, you’re not going to understand how hard it is. But if someone hasn’t done it recently themselves—you’re making a bet. It might pay off. It might not. But it’ll never make sense. Especially if you’re below $250m in revenue. Because these execs that haven’t done it for a while … well … they’ve lost touch. They’re been away too long. They forget what it takes. They start talking about strategy instead of execution. And that’s death at a startup. The second point I wanted to share is this.
